assumptions.summary: The person and water together keep the tub full, so added water produces equal overflow.
Hand motion is assumed to make the bath spatially uniform and effectively instantaneous.
Room temperature is constant at the scenario value.
Hot-water supply temperature is constant while the faucet runs.
Heat transfer through heavily insulated tub walls is neglected in the baseline.
Heat transfer between the person and water is neglected.
Overflow temperature equals the uniform bath temperature and overflow mass rate equals inflow mass rate.
Fiberglass wall effectiveness and the bubble factor are represented as assumed effective-area multipliers.

contributions.summary: Provides an answer-first two-branch strategy that separates temporal flow control from spatial mixing.
Responds to the small-scale data gap with an own-tub experiment and appendix procedure.
Builds an explicit volume/effective-area interface for transporting the cooling constant across scenarios.
Connects a hybrid event simulation to an enumerable objective and a concrete faucet recommendation.
Uses repeated CAD-plus-objective blocks for eight controlled geometry cases.
Reports the expected geometry trend as unsupported in the tested set and names a counteracting heating mechanism.
Turns the recognized manual-mixing burden into a visually specified product concept.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: External 100, 300, and 800 mL cooling series at 23 C provide three small-scale exponential fits.
Ambient shifting subtracts 23 C during fitting and restores it in the reported equations.
A 55 by 23 by 13 inch insulated tub at 21 C is measured every minute for sixty minutes from 37 C.
A four-row table records effective area, volume, and k for three beakers and the own tub.
The standard simulation uses a 60 by 30 by 14 inch tub, 37 C target, 21 C room, 48 C hot water, and forty minutes.
Eight CAD designs provide dimensions, surface areas, and volumes in two controlled scenario families.
The appendix records materials, ambient temperature, tub dimensions, fill procedure, and measurement schedule, while raw numeric readings remain represented only by the body graph.

edges.handoff: The uniform T(t) reduction makes a single Newton-cooling state usable.
Uniform mixing makes overflow temperature equal to bath temperature.
Beaker and tub exponential fits provide the four k values used in the geometry regression.
Equation 14 supplies K for the baseline simulation after unit conversion.
The equal-inflow/overflow balance supplies the per-frame heating increment.
The same event simulation and exhaustive grid search are rerun for every scenario.
The burden of continuous manual mixing motivates the device alternative.
The faucet remains the heat source while the prototype changes only spatial delivery and mixing.

feedbacks: Geometry, material, and additive outputs return through equation 14 to the same flow decision.
The limitation of manual mixing returns to the spatial branch as the Home Jacuzzi concept.
Appendices return experimental and implementation detail to the calibration and optimization claims.

independent_extensions.summary: Measure a three-dimensional temperature field and mixing timescale for hand motion and bottom jets before replacing T(x,y,z,t) by T(t).
Correct the cylinder geometry, rebuild the k data table with one time unit, and validate the geometry law on independent full-size tubs.
Derive a unit-consistent open-system energy balance and verify equation-code parity with conservation tests.
Optimize temperature error and water use jointly with faucet on/off control, uncertainty, and time-step/grid convergence.
Calibrate wall resistance and bubble-layer heat transfer from physical measurements rather than effective-area guesses.
Prototype the Home Jacuzzi and measure head loss, outlet distribution, mixing, scald risk, attachment stability, cleaning, and user effort.

models.section: A Simple Solution and Home Jacuzzi
models.summary: A single-ended faucet and buoyant hot water motivate counterclockwise hand circulation; the later perforated bottom tube is a no-hand alternative. Both routes are intended to justify a uniform bath temperature at each time.
The paper derives T=T0 exp(-kt) for temperature above ambient, corrects beaker regressions to a 23 C asymptote, and records three fitted cooling curves.
Four cases (three beakers and one tub) define X=V^2/SA_E^3; four transforms are compared and the cube-root exponential relation is selected by reported R-squared.
The paper writes separate incoming and outgoing heat terms, equates inflow and overflow mass rates under a full-tub condition, subtracts them, and connects net heat to the water mass.

The Python implementation converts geometry, computes k, applies one-minute cooling updates, permanently starts heating after a 1.4 C drop, accumulates squared deviation while water runs, and enumerates 16.00 down to 0.02 gpm by 0.01.
Eight geometry designs are evaluated in two controlled families, then fiberglass and bubble insulation are represented by effective-area transformations and compared with the standard tub.
A U-shaped perforated tube connects to the faucet, sends hot water to the bottom, and uses buoyant rise plus outlet jets to circulate the bath.

results_trace.summary: The standard case selects 1.81 gpm with deviance 10.179381314125882.
The simulation replay reports R-squared 0.999836; the direct regression reports 0.97326.
At V=25,200 in^3 and SA=1,800 in^2, the reported optimum is 1.81 gpm with deviance 10.18.
At constant volume with SA=1,680 in^2, the reported optimum is 1.61 gpm with deviance 7.86.
At constant volume with SA=1,625.81 in^2, the reported optimum is 1.95 gpm with deviance 5.16.
At constant volume with SA=1,575 in^2, the reported optimum is 4.70 gpm with deviance 1.20.
At SA=1,600 in^2 and V=24,079.82 in^3, the reported optimum is 1.58 gpm with deviance 6.44.
At constant area with V=24,000 in^3, the reported optimum is 1.60 gpm with deviance 6.67.
At constant area with V=22,400 in^3, the reported optimum is 1.41 gpm with deviance 9.00.
At constant area with V=18,200 in^3, the reported optimum is 2.15 gpm with deviance 9.35.
Neither controlled family shows a stable monotone optimum trend across the four tested designs.
The effective-area fiberglass scenario reports 7.52 gpm and deviance 1.92 versus the 1.81 gpm acrylic baseline.
The 0.95 bubble factor scenario reports 1.58 gpm and deviance 8.75.
The design outcome is a bottom-distribution tube intended to replace continuous hand mixing.

task_reconstruction.classification_basis: A is taken only from the source filename and parent folder.
deliverables: Model water temperature in space and time.
Recommend a strategy that keeps temperature uniform and near the initial value without excessive water.
Study bathtub geometry, person geometry/temperature/motion, and their interactions.
Provide a one-page nontechnical user explanation.
task_reconstruction.spatial_scale: The three-dimensional water body, reduced by the paper to one lumped temperature
task_reconstruction.stakeholder: A person bathing in an ordinary tub
task_reconstruction.time_scale: One forty-minute bath in the authors' baseline

unresolved_questions: The official task asks for T(x,y,z,t) and dependencies on person shape, volume, temperature, and motion, but the paper assumes instantaneous uniform mixing, builds only T(t), and does not subtract occupant displacement or heat capacity from the water state.

Paper-equation and implementation mismatch: equations 15 and 21 print 0.385387... instead of evaluating equation 14 for the standard bath (about 0.0001320844/s), and equation 22 multiplies by m_tub while the code divides by tub mass.

Unit and notation drift: k is called unitless despite having inverse-time units; the own-tub 0.00448/min conversion is described inconsistently; T alternates among temperature above ambient, bath temperature, and absolute temperature while code uses Celsius.

The heat ledger writes mCpT where a temperature change is intended, labels power-like inflow/outflow terms as Q or Delta Q, equates energy and rate expressions without a time step, leaves T_tub unclear, and declares Cp in code without using it.

The cylinder area formula omits a factor of two in the lateral term, equation 13 further loses geometric factors, and the table labels area in m rather than m^2; these issues can alter all three beaker effective areas and the k fit.

The geometry law uses only three beakers and one tub, selects among four transforms by in-sample R-squared, supplies no holdout or uncertainty, and reuses the own-tub data in the later R^2=0.999836 validation replay.

The official water-waste requirement is absent from the objective: equation 23 is temperature-only, code accumulates it only after water starts, zero flow is excluded, and a faucet once triggered never turns off, so 1.81 gpm is optimal only for this narrow score.

The explicit one-minute update has no step-size convergence study; cooling is applied before event detection, the threshold is delayed to a frame boundary, abs(T-T0)>1.4 has no upper shutoff, and WATER_RUNNING remains true permanently.

Fiberglass at one-eighth acrylic insulation and bubble factor 0.95 are illustrative assumptions, not calibrated material data; compressing wall conduction or a bubble layer into effective exposed area is unvalidated and cannot support universal numeric savings.

Evaporation, radiation, spatial natural/forced convection, wall and air dynamics, and body heat are omitted; eight shape cases cannot establish a universal absence of V/SA trend, and plots lack uncertainty and use differing objective scales.

verification.summary: A 23 C physical asymptote check corrects the beaker regression boundary.
Four transformations are compared through reported R-squared rather than selecting one silently.
The chosen cube-root feature reports R-squared 0.999298544362311 on the four calibration cases.
Simulation replay under the own-experiment conditions overlays prediction and observation.
The replay reports R-squared 0.999836 versus 0.97326 for the exponential comparator.
Constant-volume and constant-area families act as controlled scenario checks for geometry dependence.
The paper explicitly claims retrospective agreement and scenario accommodation, making the intended validation claim inspectable.
Executable code exposes constants, conversions, update order, event logic, grid bounds, and objective accumulation.

Water Beaker Cooling plots temperature versus minutes for 100, 300, and 800 mL series, establishing the multi-volume evidence base.
Three colored point series with exponential dashed fits and R-squared labels show the 23 C asymptote correction.
A sixty-minute raw bathtub temperature line plot exposes the large-volume observations used for calibration.
The ambient-shifted bathtub exponential regression displays the fitted decay and R-squared for the own experiment.
The first four-point plot fits k against X=V^2/SA_E^3 and reports R-squared 0.99764.
The squared-X candidate plot records a worse R-squared, preserving a rejected feature transform.
The square-root-X candidate plot records the improved 0.999294 fit.
The cube-root-X plot shows the selected exponential feature and R-squared about 0.999299.
The standard-bath deviance-flow curve marks its blue minimum on the red objective curve and supports the 1.81 gpm selection.
The temperature-time trajectory shows cooling until the threshold and heating after faucet activation.
Observed and simulated temperatures are overlaid against time with the reported R-squared 0.999836.
Eight CAD pages and their eight paired objective-curve pages (p.19-34) repeat a shape, dimensions, controlled SA/V, optimum, and deviance evidence block.
A surface-area versus optimal-flow scatter summarizes four constant-volume designs.
A volume versus optimal-flow scatter summarizes four constant-area designs and the nonmonotone in-set result.
The fiberglass deviance-flow curve marks the reported 7.52 gpm, 1.92 deviance minimum.
The bubble-bath objective curve marks the reported 1.58 gpm, 8.75 deviance minimum.
Figure 2 blueprint shows a U-shaped bottom tube and outlet holes that redistribute faucet inflow.
Figures 3 and 4 show the proposed product and its installed/use configuration, completing the prototype communication chain.
